slides.headline: 3 ADHD Myths That Even Doctors Get Wrong
slides.sub: If you've ever been told you 'don't seem like you have ADHD,' this one's for you. We're debunking three myths that kept a lot of us undiagnosed for years.

slides.headline: If you can hyperfocus, you don't have ADHD
ADHD is about regulation, not just attention
slides.body: ADHD isn't a shortage of attention — it's an inability to control where attention goes. The same brain that zones out during a meeting can lock onto a documentary for four hours without moving. Researchers call this 'hyperfocus,' and it's actually driven by the same dopamine dysregulation that causes distractibility: your brain chases stimulation it finds compelling and abandons everything it doesn't.

slides.headline: ADHD means you can't focus on anything, ever
Interest and urgency hijack the ADHD brain
slides.body: People with ADHD have what researcher Dr. William Dodson calls an 'interest-based nervous system' — attention is controlled by novelty, passion, challenge, or deadlines, not by intention or importance. That's why the report that's due tomorrow suddenly gets done at midnight, but the one due next month is invisible. It has nothing to do with caring. It has everything to do with how the ADHD brain is wired to activate.

slides.headline: You'd focus fine if you just tried harder
Effort alone cannot fix a dopamine gap
slides.body: ADHD involves measurable differences in dopamine and norepinephrine transmission in the prefrontal cortex — the region that governs sustained attention and task initiation. A 2021 meta-analysis in Neuroscience & Biobehavioral Reviews confirmed structural and functional brain differences in people with ADHD that willpower simply cannot override. Telling someone to 'just try harder' is like telling a person with low vision to squint more.

slides.headline: Your attention isn't broken. It's just different.
slides.body: Understanding the real science behind ADHD is the first step to actually working with your brain instead of against it. Save this for the next time someone tells you that you 'don't seem like you have ADHD.'
slides.commentPrompt: Which of these myths have you heard the most? Drop it below 👇

caption:
If you've ever hyperfocused for six hours straight and then wondered if your diagnosis was real — this is for you.

The biggest myth about ADHD is that it means you can never pay attention. In reality, ADHD is an attention *regulation* problem. The same brain that loses your keys also memorizes every lyric to an album it heard once.

And no, trying harder isn't the answer. ADHD involves real, measurable differences in how dopamine moves through the prefrontal cortex — differences that show up on brain scans, not just report cards.

slides.headline: Which type of task paralysis are you?
slides.sub: four types. one is painfully you. comment your letter.

slides.body: You open the project and there are seventeen things to do and you don't know which one is first so you close the tab. You stare at the list. You make a new list. You reorganize the new list. Forty minutes later, nothing has started and somehow you're reading about the history of staplers. It's not laziness — your brain genuinely cannot find an entry point when everything feels equally urgent and enormous.

Your fifth-grade teacher wrote 'doesn't turn in work' but what she missed was that you had three drafts in your notebook that weren't good enough yet. You'll start the email as soon as you know exactly what to say. The task isn't abandoned — it's being held hostage by a version of it that has to be perfect before anyone sees it. ADHD perfectionism isn't high standards, it's a fear response dressed in high standards' clothes.

You signed up for the course, bought the supplies, told two people about your plan — and then the dopamine evaporated and the whole thing feels like homework now. This has happened with pottery, podcasting, Portuguese, and that business idea from March. Your brain isn't flaky, it runs on a neurotransmitter system that requires genuine novelty or urgency to activate — and 'things you already started' rarely qualify.

You cannot start the thing until the deadline is breathing on your neck, and you know this about yourself, and it still doesn't help you start earlier. The report gets done at 1am and it's actually good, which is confusing and also exhausting. Your nervous system needs the cortisol spike of real consequences to manufacture enough activation to work — that's not a personality flaw, that's a dysregulated dopamine system doing the only thing that reliably works.

slides.headline: Whichever letter you picked
slides.body: A, B, C, and D are all the same thing at the root: an attention-regulation system that struggles to initiate without the right neurochemical conditions. None of them mean you're lazy, unmotivated, or broken. They mean your brain has a harder time generating the internal 'go' signal that other people produce automatically — and that is a clinical reality, not a character flaw.

caption:
Which type of task paralysis keeps you stuck?

Because 'just start' is genuinely useless advice when your brain can't locate the start button. Task paralysis in ADHD isn't about effort or attitude — it's a dopamine and executive function problem that shows up in at least four very distinct ways, and most of us have a primary type we live in.

The Overwhelm Freezer can't find the entry point. The Perfectionist Staller is waiting to be ready. The Novelty Chaser already mentally moved on. The Deadline Gambler needs the fire to be real and close.

slides.headline: Escape a doom-scroll spiral without hating yourself
slides.sub:
You didn't choose to lose 90 minutes to TikTok. Your brain did — and there's a way out that doesn't require willpower or a lecture.
No discipline required.

slides.headline: Name it out loud, literally
slides.body:
Say — or whisper — 'I'm in a scroll spiral.' That's it. No judgment attached.
Naming an experience activates your prefrontal cortex and creates a tiny gap between impulse and action — something ADHD brains rarely get automatically.
Example: You catch yourself 47 reels deep at midnight and you just say, 'yep, spiral.' Done.

slides.headline: Do one 10-second body interrupt
slides.body:
Stand up, press your feet into the floor, take one slow breath, and look at something across the room.
This isn't mindfulness theater — it's a pattern interrupt that briefly spikes norepinephrine, helping your brain shift attentional gears.
Example: You put your phone face-down on your chest, plant both feet flat, and just look at the ceiling fan for ten seconds.

slides.headline: Give your brain a tiny win
slides.body:
Immediately do one micro-task that takes under 60 seconds — fill a glass of water, plug in your charger, close one browser tab.
ADHD brains struggle with activation energy, but completing even a trivial task releases a small dopamine hit that makes the next move feel possible.
Example: You walk to the kitchen, fill a glass of water, and drink half of it. Your brain now has evidence that you can do things.

slides.headline: Swap, don't stop cold
slides.body:
Instead of trying to quit screens entirely, switch to a pre-chosen 'landing' app — something low-stimulation you already enjoy, like a calm playlist, a saved article, or a slow YouTube channel.
Cold-turkey stops create a dopamine cliff that almost always backfires for ADHD brains; a gentler swap keeps arousal regulated without a crash.
Example: You close Instagram and open your lo-fi playlist — same screen, completely different neurological ask.

slides.headline: Set a 'reentry' anchor, not a rule
slides.body:
Pick one specific, concrete thing you're moving toward — not 'be productive,' but 'get into bed and open my book.' Write it in your notes app before you close TikTok.
Working memory in ADHD is unreliable under high dopamine load; an external anchor offloads the cognitive work so your brain doesn't have to hold the intention alone.
Example: You type 'brush teeth → bed → first page of book' in your notes before you close the app, so future-you has a script to follow.

slides.headline: These aren't flaws. They're ADHD traits.
slides.kicker: ...this one's going to sting a little

slides.headline: Object Permanence
slides.body:
Out of sight genuinely means out of mind — not because you're careless, but because your brain doesn't passively hold objects or people in awareness the way neurotypical brains do.
You bought duplicates of something you already owned because you couldn't picture where the original was.
You haven't texted someone you love in four months and somehow didn't notice until now.
The bill sat in the drawer and your brain treated it like it didn't exist until the late notice arrived.

slides.headline: Low Interoception
slides.body:
Interoception is your brain's ability to read internal body signals — hunger, thirst, fatigue, a full bladder. In ADHD brains, that signal system is genuinely quieter.
You looked up at 4pm and realized you hadn't eaten or had water since yesterday morning.
You didn't know you were exhausted until you started crying at a commercial.
You held it for three hours because your body never sent an urgent enough message.

slides.headline: Rejection Masking
slides.body:
Rejection Sensitive Dysphoria means perceived rejection can trigger an intense, fast emotional response — so many ADHDers become expert shape-shifters just to prevent it.
You agreed to something you hated because the thought of disappointing them felt physically unbearable.
You rewrote a two-line text eleven times because one wrong word could mean they're mad at you.
You became whoever the room needed you to be and lost track of who you actually are.

slides.headline: Time Blindness
slides.body:
ADHD brains often experience time as two zones — now and not now — rather than a continuous, measurable flow. It's not rudeness. It's a neurological difference in time perception.
You were genuinely shocked that an hour had passed when it felt like ten minutes.
You showed up late to something you actually cared about, again, and hated yourself for it.
The report card said 'doesn't manage her time well' and no one asked why.

slides.headline: Emotional Permanence
slides.body:
Just as objects disappear when unseen, emotions can too — including love, safety, and confidence. When you can't feel it in the moment, your brain registers it as gone.
You needed your partner to reassure you they still loved you, even though nothing had changed.
You felt completely worthless the moment a project wasn't going well, forgetting every win before it.
When someone wasn't texting back, the anxiety wasn't 'they're busy' — it was 'they hate me now.'

slides.headline: You're not broken.
slides.body: Every trait here was explained to you as a character flaw. It wasn't. It isn't.
slides.commentPrompt: Which one hit hardest? Drop the number in the comments — I read every single one.

caption:
These aren't personality flaws. They're ADHD traits that were never explained to you.

Forgetting people exist when they're not in front of you. Missing hunger cues until you're shaking. Agreeing to things you hate because disappointing someone feels catastrophic. None of that is laziness or carelessness or being 'too sensitive' — it's a brain that works differently.

The hardest part isn't the trait itself. It's spending decades believing it was a moral failure.

Which one on this list made you stop and go 'oh'? Tell me in the comments.

slides.headline: dear diary: i just wanted to sleep

slides.body: Decided tonight is the night. Reasonable bedtime. I am a person who sleeps. I put my phone down and closed my eyes for a full four minutes before remembering I never replied to that text from March.

Just going to check one thing. The one thing was: what is the deepest lake in the world. I now know twelve facts about Lake Baikal and have watched a documentary clip about a fish that has never seen sunlight. I relate to that fish.
Okay. Phone is across the room. This is it. I am doing it. I am lying here thinking about that thing I said at a birthday party in 2014 and whether the person remembers it. They remember it.
Got up to get water. Reorganized the mugs by height. Do not know why. Did not choose this.

Still awake. Started a list of everything I need to do tomorrow, which reminded me of everything I didn't do today, which reminded me of everything I haven't done since 2019. The list is two pages. I feel terrible and also a little productive.

slides.headline: it was never laziness
slides.body: ADHD brains have a dysregulated arousal system — meaning falling asleep isn't just a decision you make, it's a neurological event your brain actively makes harder. The racing thoughts, the random tasks, the 2am shame spiral: those aren't character flaws. That's an executive function system with no off switch. You weren't failing at bedtime. You were fighting your own wiring with zero backup.

slides.headline: there's a word for that thing you do
slides.sub: when you sat down to google one thing and looked up to find it was 3am and you'd read 47 articles about the migration patterns of monarch butterflies

defs: An intense, sustained state of absorption in a task or topic — often one the brain finds novel, urgent, or deeply interesting — during which time, hunger, and outside demands fade almost entirely from awareness.
The reason you can't 'just stop' playing a video game for five minutes but also genuinely cannot start a work email for three days.
slides.example: "I was supposed to restring one guitar string. Six hours later I had reorganized my entire music collection by decade, watched four documentaries, and ordered a ukulele. I was not hungry. I was not tired. I was unreachable."

slides.headline: the 'quick search' that wasn't
slides.body: You looked up the side effects of one medication at 9pm. By midnight you had seventeen tabs open, a hand-written timeline of pharmaceutical history, and a genuine opinion about a 2009 FDA hearing. You weren't being irresponsible. Your brain found a thread and pulled — hard.

slides.headline: the project that finally clicked
slides.body: For weeks the presentation sat untouched. Then, two days before the deadline, something shifted — and you produced twelve slides, a custom color palette, and speaker notes in a single night. Your manager called it 'impressive under pressure.' You called it the only way it was ever going to happen.

slides.headline: the hobby spiral
slides.body: You picked up watercolor painting on a Tuesday. By Friday you had watched 30 hours of tutorials, bought professional-grade supplies, and could accurately explain the difference between cold-press and hot-press paper to anyone who would listen. Your family was not asking. You told them anyway.

slides.headline: naming it changes it
slides.body: For years, hyperfocus reads as proof you're 'lazy when you want to be' — because you can spend six hours on something you love and can't manage twenty minutes on something you don't. But hyperfocus isn't a choice or a character flaw; it's a dysregulation of attention, not a demonstration of selective effort. When you have the word, you stop explaining yourself with apologies and start building structure around how your brain actually works.

slides.headline: now you have the word
slides.body: use it. share it. save it for the next time someone says 'well you managed to focus when it was something you wanted to do.'
slides.commentPrompt: What word would YOU add to the ADHD dictionary? Drop it in the comments — we might just make it next week's slide.

caption:
There's actually a clinical name for the six-hour wikipedia spiral you can't explain to your boss.

Hyperfocus is one of the most misunderstood parts of ADHD — because from the outside it looks like proof you could 'try harder all along.' It's not. It's your brain's attention regulation doing the opposite of what you need, locking on instead of letting go, and it runs on interest and urgency — not intention.

It's why you can rebuild a computer from scratch but cannot send a two-sentence reply email. Both are real. Neither cancels the other out.

slides.headline: you don't need to plan the perfect week
slides.sub: Sunday isn't a productivity tool. It's just a day.

slides.headline: the blank planner is not a failure
slides.body: Leaving it empty is a valid choice your brain can make.

slides.headline: rest doesn't have to be earned first
slides.body: You don't owe anyone a productive week before you recover.

slides.headline: one thing is enough to start with
slides.body: Not a system. Not a routine. Just one small next thing.

slides.headline: your brain needs slack not schedules
slides.body: Unstructured time isn't wasted — it's how ADHD brains decompress.

slides.headline: your permission slip for this week
slides.body: You are allowed to skip the Sunday reset ritual entirely.

slides.headline: see you monday
slides.body: same brain. no new you required.

caption:
you don't need to plan the perfect week.

The pressure to use Sunday as a launch pad — color-coded schedule, meal prep, inbox zero — is real. And for ADHD brains, that pressure usually ends in a paralysis spiral on the couch at 9pm feeling behind before Monday even starts.

You're not lazy. You're dysregulated. There's a difference.

This week, the bar is low and that's on purpose. One thing counts. Showing up halfway counts. Resting without justifying it counts.
